overview: The file contains American Consul John Carter Vincent’s report on the Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference held at Dairen on August 15–17, 1933, together with a translated newspaper version of Lieutenant General Kuniaki Koiso’s principal address. Vincent portrays the gathering as a largely ceremonial exercise intended to impress Manchurian delegates and promote a Japan–Manchukuo economic bloc, noting that its closed committees apparently produced few concrete results, although Japanese commercial interests privately pressed for lower Manchukuo tariffs. Koiso’s speech presents the Kwantung Army’s economic vision for Manchukuo, including integrated transport, road and river development, cotton cultivation, colonization, mining, timber, heavy industry, and the abolition of extraterritoriality.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports on the proceedings, political purpose, and limited accomplishments of the Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference held at Dairen on August 15–17, 1933.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports that approximately 120 Manchurian delegates and Japanese participants, principally from Dairen, Osaka, and Nagoya, attended a conference dominated by speeches, sightseeing, and six closed committee meetings. He regards Koiso’s opening address on a Japan–Manchukuo economic bloc as the conference’s most significant statement and characterizes the remaining presentations as familiar propaganda or instruction for the Manchurian delegates. Although the committees apparently achieved little, Japanese commercial delegates privately pressed Manchukuo officials for lower import duties. Vincent concludes that the event succeeded chiefly as a demonstration of the orderly development of the Kwantung territory intended to impress the visiting delegates.

subfiles.title: Translation of Koiso’s speech on the Japan–Manchukuo economic bloc
subfiles.doc_type: enclosure: translated newspaper article and speech
subfiles.to: Delegates to the Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference
subfiles.about: Sets out the Kwantung Army commander’s program for integrating and developing the economies of Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Koiso argues that Japan and Manchukuo are mutually indispensable in both military and economic terms and should form a complementary economic bloc rather than reproduce Japanese capitalism wholesale in Manchuria. He emphasizes communications development, including cheaper rail freight, improved rivers and highways, 5,000 kilometres of new roads in the current year, and an eventual network of 60,000 kilometres. He also discusses cotton cultivation intended to replace Japanese imports from America and India, selective colonization, mining and timber development, the abolition of extraterritoriality, and expansion of coal, gas, electricity, glass, cement, and iron industries. The speech closes by defending the Army against accusations of autocracy and subordinating private interests to the perceived survival of Japan and Manchuria.

interest: The file juxtaposes the American consul’s skeptical, observational account with the Kwantung Army commander’s expansive public vision, making it especially useful for comparing diplomatic assessment with Japanese colonial propaganda. Vincent’s distinction between the conference’s ceremonial success and its lack of substantive decisions illuminates how economic conferences could function as political theater. Koiso’s detailed references to transport targets, import substitution, colonization, resource exploitation, and industrial policy provide a concise statement of the developmental and strategic logic behind Japan’s occupation of Manchuria.
